ca_pratt_s_crack_dihedrals_area.blurb: A steep granite wall in Scheelite Canyon, a side canyon off Pine Creek west of Bishop, visible from the canyon floor and built around a pair of big pale dihedrals. Eleven routes mix trad cracks and corners with bolted lines, running from 5.9 through the 5.10s and 5.11s, then up into 5.13 and a couple of harder bolted pitches. Several climbs are long, roughly 300 feet, so expect multi-pitch outings with rappel or walk-off descents. The climbing rewards finger and hand jamming and tidy footwork more than raw power. The wall faces south, so it soaks up sun; start early on warm days.
ca_pratt_s_crack_dihedrals_area.parking_note: From the Pine Creek road, drive 7.7 miles up the canyon and turn right onto a dirt track directly opposite the campground. It splits almost at once; take the right fork and continue a couple of hundred yards to the small parking area. The surface can be rutted and loose after rain.

ca_south_pile.blurb: A small, lower-key pile of rock at the southern end of the cirque of formations just inside the Alabama Hills, near Lone Pine in the Eastern Sierra. It holds eleven short routes, nine bolted and two trad, with most of the grades falling between 5.6 and 5.8 and a handful of 5.10s. The setting is the draw: easy access, wide views and belays that sit practically beside the car. It makes a handy quick stop for newer leaders and anyone warming up before heading to the bigger Alabama Hills walls.

ca_slab_city_right.blurb: The right-hand section of Slab City, one of the sectors of the Riverside Quarry in the Inland Empire. All eleven routes are bolted and between 50 and 70 feet long, with the bulk sitting in the 5.10s, one easier 5.7, a lone 5.11 and two 5.12s. The rock is smooth and slabby with the odd crack, so the climbing is about delicate footwork and balance rather than power. Some lines start partway up a talus slope, which means a little scrambling in the approach. It is a short walk from the parking area.

ca_school_rock_west_face.blurb: The west-facing side of School Rock, a roughly 60-foot formation on a hillside above Running Springs in the San Bernardino Mountains. Ten of the eleven routes are trad and one is set up as a top rope, running from 5.5 up to 5.12 with the heaviest cluster at 5.9. Cracks and clean, compact stone make for a good place to practise placing gear. Facing west, it bakes in the afternoon, so summer mornings and spring or fall afternoons are the comfortable windows. It can be climbed much of the year when snow stays off the road, and rattlesnakes are around in warm weather.
ca_school_rock_west_face.parking_note: Between Running Springs and the Keller Peak turnoff, head up Running Springs School Road for 0.8 miles to a gated dirt road on the left, and leave the car there.

ca_upper_theology_crag.blurb: A steep sandstone crag up Mission Canyon above Santa Barbara, a hike beyond the Seven Falls area that takes about 30 to 40 minutes. Eleven routes, nine bolted and two set up for top rope, are mostly vertical to overhanging and lean hard: most are 5.11 and 5.12, with a few 5.9 and 5.10 lines. Most of the face stays in shade all day, which makes it a cool choice in warm weather and chilly in winter. The walk goes up the creek bed and over a ridge, and a big carving from the early 1900s marks the base.

ca_south_face_8.blurb: The sunny side of North Rock, one of the ocean-edge sandstone formations at Footsteps Rock on the far northwest coast of California. Eleven routes, mostly bolted with a few trad and top-rope options, run from 5.9 through the 5.10s and into the 5.11s and 5.12s, with pocketed faces and arete climbing beneath a bulge. The north side of the same formation is cooler, but this one catches the sun. Bolts at this coastal spot can be old, so check them carefully. The trail down ends at a notch above the formations.

ca_egg_the_2.blurb: A big egg-shaped boulder beside the ocean at Mickey's Beach on the Marin coast, north of Stinson Beach. Ten sport routes and one top rope cover a wide range, from an easy 5.6 through the 5.10s to a hard group of 5.11s and 5.12s. There is no trad. The east side holds the gentler, shorter slabs, which tend to stay shaded and suit beginners, while the north side has longer, pumpy lines with hard starts. Anchors are sparse, so bring extra slings for building a top rope. The walk down is short but steep, and a beach lies beyond.
